---
title: "Choosing a map scale"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.2, dpi = 100,
  fig.retina = 2, dev = "ragg_png", out.width = "100%"
)
options(gglaplot2.font = "inter")
library(ggplot2)
library(sf)
library(gglaplot2)
```

A choropleth puts every area into one of a few bins and colours it by the
bin, so the scale decides what the map says before any colour is chosen.
`scale_fill_gla_b()` cuts equal steps by default, and that is the right
scale for most published maps. This page is about the other choice, a scale
classed by the distribution of the data, which [Maps](maps.html) and
[Mapping a change](diverging-maps.html) leave aside: what each method
shows, how to ask for one, and when not to.

The data is real: the Leave share in the 2016 referendum by London borough,
which runs from 21% in the City of London to 70% in Havering, with most
boroughs between 30% and 50%.

```{r data}
leave <- merge(gla_boroughs, EURef[, c("Area_Code", "Leave", "PropLeave")],
               by.x = "code", by.y = "Area_Code")
leave$margin <- leave$PropLeave - 50
summary(leave$PropLeave)
```

## Equal steps, the default

Five bins of one width, from a round number at or below the data. A step of
colour is a step of ten points everywhere on the map, and the same value
takes the same colour on next year's map, which is what makes the default
the right scale for a series.

```{r equal}
map <- function(fill, scale, title) {
  ggplot(leave) +
    geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = {{ fill }})) +
    scale +
    gla_labs(title = title, subtitle = "Share voting Leave, 2016",
             source = "Electoral Commission") +
    theme_gla_map()
}
map(PropLeave, scale_fill_gla_b(name = NULL, steps = 5, labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)),
    "Equal steps of ten points")
```

The cost shows when the data is skewed or one area sits far from the rest:
the steps have to reach the extremes, so most areas crowd into one or two
bins and the map goes flat where the reader wants the detail.

## Classing by the data

`method` cuts the bins by the distribution instead. Each method decides
which areas share a bin; the package then draws the lines between the bins
by one rule, described further down, so that no area is moved by rounding
and the legend reads cleanly.

```{r jenks}
map(PropLeave, scale_fill_gla_b(name = NULL, method = "jenks", steps = 5,
                                labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)),
    "Natural breaks (Jenks)")
```

`gla_class_breaks()` is the same calculation on its own. Its `counts` say
how many areas each bin holds, which is the quickest way to see what a
method did.

```{r counts}
gla_class_breaks(leave$PropLeave, "jenks", n = 5)
```

### What each method shows

```{r methods, fig.show = "hold", out.width = "50%", fig.width = 5, fig.height = 4.2}
methods <- c(jenks = "Natural breaks", quantile = "Quantiles", boxplot = "Box plot",
             sd = "Standard deviations", headtails = "Head and tail", geometric = "Geometric")
for (m in names(methods)) {
  print(
    ggplot(leave) +
      geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = PropLeave)) +
      scale_fill_gla_b(name = NULL, method = m, steps = 5,
                       labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)) +
      gla_labs(title = methods[[m]]) +
      theme_gla_map()
  )
}
```

- **Natural breaks** (`"jenks"`) finds the grouping that keeps the areas in
  each bin as alike as possible. An area far from the rest usually gets a
  bin of its own, and the bins fall where the data has gaps. The general
  choice for a one-off map.
- **Quantiles** (`"quantile"`) put the same number of areas in each bin,
  so the map is evenly coloured whatever the distribution. The cost is
  that an outlier is hidden among its neighbours, and two areas a tenth of
  a point apart can be in different bins while two far apart share one.
- **Box plot** (`"boxplot"`) cuts at the quartiles and sets apart anything
  beyond the fences, 1.5 times the interquartile range past them. An
  outlier gets its own bin by a fixed rule, so the bin appears only when
  there is one. The number of bins comes from the data, not `steps`.
- **Standard deviations** (`"sd"`) cuts bins one standard deviation wide
  around the mean, for a measure that is roughly normal. The number of
  bins comes from the data; bins no area falls in are not drawn.
- **Head and tail** (`"headtails"`) is for a heavy tail, a few large values
  and many small: it splits at the mean, then the upper part at its mean,
  and so on while the upper part is the minority. The small values share
  one broad bin and each step up holds fewer areas.
- **Geometric** (`"geometric"`) widens the bins by a constant ratio from the
  smallest value to the largest, for counts and densities that span orders
  of magnitude. It needs values above zero, so it suits the number of votes
  rather than the share.

```{r geometric}
map(Leave, scale_fill_gla_b(name = NULL, method = "geometric", steps = 5,
                            labels = label_gla_number()),
    "Leave votes, geometric bins") +
  labs(subtitle = "Votes for Leave, 2016")
```

Five bins were asked for and three drawn: two of the five would hold no
borough, since nothing sits between the City's 1,100 votes and the next
borough's 17,000. A bin no area falls in is never drawn, whichever method,
so the count is at most `steps`, not always `steps`.

## A change, classed each side of zero

On a diverging scale each side is classed on its own, with its own count,
and zero (or `midpoint`) is always a break. `steps = c(3, 3)` is the
default; here the margin over 50% is classed three bins a side.

```{r diverging}
ggplot(leave) +
  geom_gla_sf(aes(fill = margin)) +
  scale_fill_gla_b("diverging", name = NULL, method = "jenks",
                   labels = label_gla_percent(scale = 1)) +
  gla_labs(title = "Margin for Leave, natural breaks each side of 50%",
           subtitle = "Percentage points above or below 50%, 2016",
           source = "Electoral Commission") +
  theme_gla_map()
```

A side with fewer distinct values than bins gets one bin per value, and
a method that works on size, head and tail and geometric, reads the side
below the midpoint by the size of the fall.

## Where the lines are drawn

A method says which areas share a bin. It does not say where the legend's
numbers should be, and left to itself each method writes its break on a
data value: natural breaks on the top member of each class, so a class of
one value has no width and vanishes from the legend, and quantiles at
figures like 38.39%. The package writes every break by one rule instead:

1. Each break goes in the gap between two neighbouring classes.
2. All the breaks are rounded to the coarsest precision at which every one
   still sits inside its gap: whole numbers if they do, else one decimal
   place, else two. On the Leave share that is whole percentages. Rounding
   therefore never moves an area to another bin.
3. The limits widen to that precision, unless `limits` were set.
4. The legend prints at that precision, and the hover of an interactive map
   one figure finer.

So the legend's numbers are where the lines are drawn, chosen for reading,
and the classes are the method's. One consequence is worth knowing: a bin
labelled "22% to 36%" means its areas fall between those lines, not that
they spread across the range. With natural breaks they may all sit near
one end.

## Cautions for a map that is published again

Classed breaks are computed from the data in front of the scale. That is
their point, and it is the reason to be careful with them.

- **The scale moves with the distribution.** Next month's data gives next
  month's breaks. A borough can change colour with no change in its value,
  and an unchanged borough can look like it moved. Two classed maps side by
  side, or one issue against the last, do not compare unless the breaks
  are the same. For a series, keep the default equal steps and fix the
  frame with `limits` (and `steps`), or set `breaks` by hand, and the same
  value takes the same colour every time.
- **Say which method the map uses.** The note should name it, since a
  reader who knows the methods will read the map differently under each.
  `gla_labs(note = "Bins are natural breaks in this month's data")` is
  enough.
- **The legend is not a scale of the measure.** With equal steps a reader
  can see that a step of colour is a step of ten points. Under a classed
  scale the bins are unequal, so the colour ramp orders the areas but does
  not measure the gaps between them. Say so if the readers will not know.
- **Quantiles hide outliers and natural breaks make them.** Pick the method
  for the finding: quantiles when the point is the ranking, natural breaks
  or the box plot when the point is that one area stands apart.
- **An area beyond `limits` is classed at the edge.** With `limits` set the
  values beyond them are squished first and the legend labels the end bin
  "Below" or "Above", as it does for equal steps, and the note should name
  the area.
- **Small numbers and suppression.** A measure with many zeros or
  suppressed cells gives a class of zeros that is not a finding. Class the
  areas with a value, or use equal steps.
- **Few areas.** Across the 33 boroughs five bins is already six or seven
  areas each; more bins than that is reading detail into noise. Across
  wards and small areas the methods come into their own.

The short version: a classed scale is for the one-off read of this month's
distribution, where the finding is how the areas group; equal steps with
fixed limits are for anything that will be read against another map.

## Using the breaks elsewhere

`gla_class_breaks()` returns the breaks with their `limits`, the `digits`
they were rounded to and the `counts` per bin, so the same classes can go
into a table beside the map, a report's text, or another tool.

```{r elsewhere}
b <- gla_class_breaks(leave$margin, "jenks", n = c(3, 3), midpoint = 0)
b
attr(b, "counts")
```
